# Snowfall — Official Experimental Theme and Theme Capability Reference

> **Status: one of the official themes shipped with Sidebar, and at the same time an experimental, demonstrative theme.**
>
> Snowfall is not just a different color scheme. It is a runnable reference for what a theme can do: load an external assembly, instantiate custom controls directly from a plain XAML resource dictionary, paint a self-drawn animation into Sidebar's visual tree, expose parameters to theme authors, and follow the Windows light/dark preference. Reading it is more direct than reading a document that only lists resource keys.

> Visual direction: dark mode is a snowy-night blue gradient with white snowfall; light mode is a brighter ice-blue gradient. The actual result is drawn at runtime by `Theme.xaml` and `SnowfallOverlay`.

---

## 1. What it is, and what it is not

**It is:**

- A complete Sidebar theme: `Theme.xaml` defines colors, backgrounds, Flyout, drag window, notifications, and tile interaction styles.
- A separate assembly, `WindowsModern.SnowFall.dll`, containing the self-drawn snow control, the decorator, and the palette provider.
- A reference implementation where a theme and code work together: the theme XAML references types in the assembly, and the assembly reads the system theme state in return.
- A template you can copy, rename, and recolor as the starting point for your own theme.

**It is not:**

- Part of Sidebar core. Deleting the whole theme folder does not prevent Sidebar from starting.
- A general-purpose animation library. The snow only serves this theme's visual language.
- A rule that every theme must follow. It deliberately demonstrates edge capabilities; an ordinary theme can still be pure XAML.
- A pixel-fixed skin. Snow count, color, speed, and light/dark palettes are all adjustable.

---

## 2. What it demonstrates

| Capability | How it works | Key file |
|---|---|---|
| A theme loads an external assembly | `xmlns:snow="clr-namespace:WindowsModern.SnowFall;assembly=WindowsModern.SnowFall"` triggers assembly resolution | Top of `Theme.xaml` |
| Instantiate a custom control from theme XAML | `<snow:SnowfallOverlay ... />` is used directly as a child of the `SidebarBackground` and `FlyoutBackground` templates | `Theme.xaml` |
| Self-drawn animation without WPF Storyboards | `SnowfallOverlay` drives `OnRender` with a `DispatcherTimer(33 ms)` and draws ellipses every frame | `SnowFall/SnowfallOverlay.cs` |
| Parameterization through dependency properties | Snow count, size, speed, wind, sway, opacity, and color are all DPs and can be set in XAML like ordinary properties | `SnowFall/SnowfallOverlay.cs` |
| A reusable visual-tree decorator | `SnowfallHost` is a `Grid`; put any content inside it, and the snow layer is automatically placed on top | `SnowFall/SnowfallHost.cs` |
| Theme colors follow the system | `SnowfallThemeProvider` reads the Windows personalization registry, listens for preference changes, and refreshes bindings through `INotifyPropertyChanged` | `SnowFall/SnowfallThemeProvider.cs` |
| Left/right adaptation | When the sidebar is reversed, the template root grid is mirrored with `ScaleTransform ScaleX="-1"`, so the snow and wind flip with it | The `DataTrigger` in `Theme.xaml` |
| Coexistence with plugin tiles | The theme overrides global brushes and interaction styles; plugin tiles keep their own layout and consume theme colors through `DynamicResource` | `Theme.xaml` plus each tile's resource keys |

## 3. How it runs

### 3.1 How the theme is loaded

At startup, Sidebar scans `Themes` and `Gadgets` under the program directory:

```text
Sidebar.exe
├── Themes/
│   └── WindowsModern.SnowFall/
│       ├── Theme.xaml
│       ├── Locale.xml
│       ├── Mkho-Christmas-Snow-flake.ico
│       ├── README.md
│       ├── README.en.md
│       ├── WindowsModern.SnowFall.dll
│       └── WindowsModern.SnowFall.pdb
└── Gadgets/
```

`Theme.xaml` under `Themes` is a `ResourceDictionary`. When XAML reaches:

```xml
xmlns:snow="clr-namespace:WindowsModern.SnowFall;assembly=WindowsModern.SnowFall"
```

WPF asks to load `WindowsModern.SnowFall`. `CurrentDomain_AssemblyResolve` in `App.xaml.cs` then:

1. Looks for a DLL with the same name in the recursive index of `Themes` and `Gadgets`.
2. If that fails, looks for `<assembly>.dll` next to `Sidebar.exe`.
3. Keeps the index for about 10 minutes; if you install a theme while Sidebar is running, restart Sidebar.

Therefore, **the DLL can simply live in the theme folder**; it does not need to be copied next to `Sidebar.exe`. The old instruction saying it "must be copied to the exe directory" is obsolete. The fallback path only matters when you put the DLL outside `Themes`/`Gadgets`.

### 3.2 Repository layout

```text
Sidebar/
├── SnowFall/                              # standalone assembly source
│   ├── SnowFall.csproj
│   ├── SnowfallOverlay.cs
│   ├── SnowfallHost.cs
│   ├── SnowfallThemeProvider.cs
│   ├── Snowflake.cs
│   └── Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs
└── Sidebar/Themes/WindowsModern.SnowFall/ # theme package
    ├── Theme.xaml
    ├── Locale.xml
    ├── README.md
    ├── README.en.md
    └── Mkho-Christmas-Snow-flake.ico
```

After a build, the DLL and PDB appear in `Debug/Themes/WindowsModern.SnowFall/` or `Release/Themes/WindowsModern.SnowFall/`. The theme's XAML, locale file, and icon are copied to the output directory as Content by the main project.

### 3.3 Building

You need Visual Studio 2015 (C# 6.0) and .NET Framework 4.0. `SnowFall.csproj` is part of `Sidebar.sln`.

```bat
"C:\Program Files (x86)\MSBuild\14.0\Bin\MSBuild.exe" ^
  SnowFall\SnowFall.csproj /t:Build /p:Configuration=Debug
```

For Release:

```bat
"C:\Program Files (x86)\MSBuild\14.0\Bin\MSBuild.exe" ^
  SnowFall\SnowFall.csproj /t:Build /p:Configuration=Release
```

The output paths are fixed by the project file:

```text
..\Debug\Themes\WindowsModern.SnowFall\
..\Release\Themes\WindowsModern.SnowFall\
```

If you build only `Sidebar.csproj`, the main project copies the theme package but does **not** build the `SnowFall` assembly for you. On a first build, or after cleaning the output, build `SnowFall` first, or build the whole solution.

### 3.4 Installing and switching

1. Copy the entire `Sidebar/Themes/WindowsModern.SnowFall/` folder into the runtime `Themes/WindowsModern.SnowFall/`.
2. Make sure `WindowsModern.SnowFall.dll` is inside that folder.
3. Start Sidebar and select **Snowfall** in the theme list.
4. If Sidebar is already running, restart it once so the assembly index cache is refreshed.

## 4. Visual structure

### 4.1 Sidebar background

The `SidebarBackground` template in `Theme.xaml` is essentially two layers: a gradient base and a snow overlay.

```xml
<Grid x:Name="RootGrid" Background="Transparent"
      RenderTransformOrigin="0.5,0.5" ClipToBounds="True">
    <Grid.RenderTransform>
        <ScaleTransform ScaleX="1" />
    </Grid.RenderTransform>

    <!-- 1. Snowy-night blue gradient -->
    <Border>
        <Border.Background>
            <LinearGradientBrush StartPoint="0,0" EndPoint="1,1">
                <GradientStop Offset="0"
                    Color="{Binding SidebarBgStartColor,
                        Source={x:Static snow:SnowfallThemeProvider.Instance}}" />
                <GradientStop Offset="1"
                    Color="{Binding SidebarBgEndColor,
                        Source={x:Static snow:SnowfallThemeProvider.Instance}}" />
            </LinearGradientBrush>
        </Border.Background>
    </Border>

    <!-- 2. Self-drawn snow layer -->
    <snow:SnowfallOverlay
        SnowflakeCount="75"
        SnowflakeSize="2.4"
        SpeedFactor="1.0"
        Wind="0.15"
        SwayFactor="1.2"
        BaseOpacity="0.9"
        SnowColor="#FFFFFFFF" />
</Grid>
```

- The gradient runs from top-left to bottom-right: deep snowy-night blue in dark mode, brighter ice blue in light mode.
- The snow layer is added last, so it sits above the gradient. It does not intercept the mouse, so tile clicks still work.
- The template root grid sets `ClipToBounds`, so snow is not drawn outside the Sidebar bounds.

### 4.2 Flyout background

`FlyoutBackground` uses a separate `SnowfallOverlay` with more restrained parameters:

```xml
<snow:SnowfallOverlay
    SnowflakeCount="30"
    SnowflakeSize="2.0"
    SpeedFactor="0.9"
    Wind="0.12"
    SwayFactor="1.0"
    BaseOpacity="0.9"
    SnowColor="#FFFFFFFF" />
```

The Flyout border uses `CornerRadius="0"` to match the square edges of the tiles. The snow layer still does not participate in hit testing.

### 4.3 Left/right mirroring

Sidebar supports both the left and right side of the screen. The theme uses the same trigger on several template root grids:

```xml
<DataTrigger Binding="{StaticResource UtilSidebarIsReversedBinding}" Value="True">
    <Setter TargetName="RootGrid" Property="RenderTransform">
        <Setter.Value>
            <ScaleTransform ScaleX="-1" />
        </Setter.Value>
    </Setter>
</DataTrigger>
```

After mirroring, the snow's fall direction, horizontal wind, and highlight edges all flip with it. No code needs to check which side the sidebar is on.

---

## 5. Tunable parameters

`SnowfallOverlay` and `SnowfallHost` expose the same set of dependency properties.

| Property | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `SnowflakeCount` | `int` | `60` | Number of snowflakes. The theme uses 75 for the Sidebar and 30 for the Flyout. |
| `SnowflakeSize` | `double` | `2.0` | Base diameter in pixels; each flake's actual size is randomized between `0.5×` and `1.6×`. |
| `SpeedFactor` | `double` | `1.0` | Fall-speed multiplier; internally clamped to a lower bound. |
| `Wind` | `double` | `0.1` | Horizontal wind; `0` falls straight down, positive values drift right. |
| `SwayFactor` | `double` | `1.0` | Left/right sway amplitude multiplier. |
| `BaseOpacity` | `double` | `0.85` | Maximum opacity; each flake's actual value is multiplied by a random `0.55–1.0` factor. |
| `SnowColor` | `Color` | `#F0F6FF` | Snow color (ARGB). The theme uses pure white. |
| `SnowflakeStrokeColor` | `Color?` | `null` | Optional stroke color. When set, a slightly larger stroke circle is drawn first, then the snow core; useful on light backgrounds. |

Useful combinations:

```xml
<!-- Quiet and sparse -->
<snow:SnowfallOverlay SnowflakeCount="30" SnowflakeSize="1.8"
                      SpeedFactor="0.8" BaseOpacity="0.75" />

<!-- Blizzard -->
<snow:SnowfallOverlay SnowflakeCount="140" SnowflakeSize="3.0"
                      SpeedFactor="1.6" Wind="0.45" SwayFactor="1.6" />

<!-- Light background: add a stroke -->
<snow:SnowfallOverlay SnowColor="#FFFFFFFF"
                      SnowflakeStrokeColor="#802A4268" />
```

---

## 6. Overlaying snow on arbitrary content with SnowfallHost

`SnowfallHost` is a `Grid` decorator. Its constructor adds the snow layer first and sets its `ZIndex` to `1000`; content added later naturally sits below the snow.

```xml
<snow:SnowfallHost SnowflakeCount="30" SnowflakeSize="1.8"
                   SpeedFactor="0.9" Wind="0.1">
    <Grid>
        <!-- Your own Flyout / Notification / custom panel -->
    </Grid>
</snow:SnowfallHost>
```

Notes:

- `SnowfallHost` is an overlay approach; it does not change content layout. The content is still measured at its own size.
- The snow layer has `IsHitTestVisible="False"`, so buttons, scrollbars, and context menus still work.
- If the content itself is opaque, the snow will be hidden behind it. To make the snow visible, leave transparent areas in the content background, or place `SnowfallHost` outside the content and make the content background semi-transparent.
- Do not nest multiple `SnowfallHost` instances in one window; that stacks multiple timers and is bad for both visuals and performance.

---

## 7. Palette and dark mode

`SnowfallThemeProvider` is a singleton exposed as `Instance`. It does three things:

1. Reads the registry:
   ```text
   HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Themes\Personalize
       SystemUsesLightTheme
       AppsUseLightTheme
   ```
   A value of `0` is treated as dark and `1` as light; if the value cannot be read, light is assumed.
2. Subscribes to `SystemEvents.UserPreferenceChanged`; the callback returns to the UI thread before reading the values again.
3. Raises `INotifyPropertyChanged` so every `{Binding ... Source={x:Static snow:SnowfallThemeProvider.Instance}}` refreshes.

Exposed state:

- `IsShellDark`: whether the shell (taskbar/Start menu) is dark.
- `IsAppDark`: whether the app theme is dark.

The color properties are grouped as follows:

- Text: `ForegroundColor`, `ForegroundSoftColor`
- Borders/edges: `BorderColor`, `EdgeColor`
- Splitters: `SplitTopColor`, `SplitBottomColor`, `SplitTopHoverColor`, `SplitBottomHoverColor`
- Arrow buttons: `ArrowColor`, `ArrowHoverColor`, `ArrowPressedColor`
- Interaction: `HoverColor`, `HoverStrongColor`
- Backgrounds: `SidebarBgStartColor`, `SidebarBgEndColor`, `TaskbarBgStartColor`, `TaskbarBgEndColor`, `FlyoutBgStartColor`, `FlyoutBgEndColor`, `DragBgColor`, `NotifBgColor`, `NotifTextBgColor`
- Clock shadow: `ClockShadowColor`

In the current implementation, **the palette follows `IsShellDark`**; `IsAppDark` is exposed as state only and does not participate in color selection. This keeps the Sidebar's snowy-night background consistent with the taskbar/Start menu, avoiding a background jump when the shell is dark but the app theme is light.

`Theme.xaml` binds only to `Color`, never directly to `Brush`:

```xml
<SolidColorBrush x:Key="GlobalForegroundBrush"
    Color="{Binding ForegroundColor,
        Source={x:Static snow:SnowfallThemeProvider.Instance}}" />
```

This avoids creating or freezing a `Brush` on the wrong thread; WPF regenerates the brush when the color changes.

---

## 8. Customizing this theme

### 8.1 Changing the palette

Prefer changing the two color sets (dark/light branches) in `SnowfallThemeProvider.cs` over hard-coding values in `Theme.xaml`. That keeps the theme consistent when the system theme changes.

If you only want to change this theme and do not plan to reuse the assembly, you can replace the bindings in `Theme.xaml` with fixed colors. Keep in mind that the Flyout, drag window, and notification window share the palette, so one change affects several windows.

### 8.2 Changing the amount of snow

Change `SnowflakeCount` / `SnowflakeSize` on the two `SnowfallOverlay` instances in `Theme.xaml`. Suggested ranges:

- Sidebar: 30–150 flakes; above 150 the drawing cost becomes noticeable on low-end machines.
- Flyout: 15–50 flakes; the Flyout area is small, and too many flakes look crowded.
- If you only want a static atmosphere, set `SnowflakeCount` to `0`; the timer still starts but no snow is drawn. A cleaner option is to remove the `SnowfallOverlay` element entirely.

### 8.3 Changing animation behavior

`SnowfallOverlay` uses a fixed 33 ms frame interval (about 30 FPS). To change speed, adjust `SpeedFactor` first rather than the timer interval: a smaller interval increases UI-thread pressure, while a larger one makes the animation choppy.

Each flake's initial size, speed, sway phase, and opacity are randomized in `ResetFlake`; `RebuildFlakes` rebuilds the flake pool when the size or a structural property changes.

### 8.4 A pitfall with visual-state animations

The `TileIconItemButtonStyle` / `TileIconItemWithTextButtonStyle` styles in the theme use `ObjectAnimationUsingKeyFrames`. WPF's `DiscreteObjectKeyFrame` does not go through `BrushConverter`, so:

```xml
<!-- Wrong: the string is not a Brush object -->
<DiscreteObjectKeyFrame KeyTime="0" Value="#3370A8D8" />

<!-- Correct: reference a shared Brush -->
<DiscreteObjectKeyFrame KeyTime="0"
    Value="{StaticResource SnowTileHoverBackground}" />
```

`ColorAnimation` is not affected because it operates on the `Color` sub-property and goes through `ColorConverter`; color animations in `TileSplliterTemplate` and `SidebarOptionsSplliterTemplate` can continue to use color strings.

### 8.5 Performance boundaries

- Snowflakes are ellipses drawn in `OnRender` every frame, not WPF animation objects. There is no Storyboard and no per-flake `FrameworkElement`.
- The timer runs only while the control is `Loaded`, visible, and has a non-zero size; it stops on `Unloaded` or when the control becomes invisible.
- Drawing uses `SolidColorBrush` instances cached by opacity bucket, avoiding a new brush every frame.
- The real cost is `SnowflakeCount × frame rate`; if you see stutter, reduce the count first, then `SnowflakeSize`.

---

## 9. Design boundaries and known limitations

- **Not a 3D/physics simulation**: flakes only fall at constant speed, sway sinusoidally, and drift with the wind. There is no collision, accumulation, or melting.
- **Does not change layout**: `SnowfallOverlay` is an overlay and does not participate in measurement; it does not push content aside.
- **Does not intercept input**: this is both an advantage and a limitation. If you want clickable snowflakes, you need to change `IsHitTestVisible` and implement hit testing yourself.
- **Multi-monitor/multi-window**: each Sidebar/Flyout instance owns its own timer; more windows mean more total drawing.
- **Theme switching**: `SnowfallThemeProvider` is a singleton whose lifetime follows the process; it does not automatically `Dispose` when the theme is unloaded. The current implementation assumes only one Snowfall theme instance is used in a Sidebar process.
- **DPI**: snowflake sizes use WPF device-independent units and follow system DPI when scaled; there is no separate DPI-awareness logic.
- **Accessibility**: the purely decorative animation has no "reduce motion" switch; if the system enables "reduce animations", the current implementation does not automatically degrade.

## 12. One-sentence summary

Snowfall extends a "theme" from a color table into a small executable visual layer: **XAML owns structure and bindings, the assembly owns drawing and system state, and Sidebar attaches both to the real visual tree**. Treat it as a reference, not a rule; you can borrow one layer, or replace all three with your own implementation.
